title: PKCE is mandatory on every authorisation-code exchange and the S256 method is the sole accepted challenge
context: PKCE (RFC 7636) protects the authorisation-code flow against code interception. The mechanism defines two challenge methods: `plain` (the verifier is used as the challenge unchanged) and `S256` (the challenge is BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier))). `plain` erodes the protection to nil in the presence of any component that can observe the challenge on the wire; the specification recommends S256 for that reason. A blueprint that accepts `plain` when a provider offers it is a foot-gun in every environment where the front channel is not fully trusted.
decision: Every authorisation redirect this blueprint mints declares `code_challenge_method=S256`. The flow controller refuses to construct a redirect without a challenge and refuses to accept a callback whose stored pending-flow does not carry a matching S256-derived challenge for the verifier the token exchange presents. A provider whose configuration would require `plain` (or that does not enforce PKCE binding at all) is a project-level ADR conversation, not a config-flag flip: the operator supersedes this ADR with a project-level ADR that accepts the erosion for their specific environment, or the operator picks a different provider.
consequences: The state machine is single-branched on PKCE: mint verifier, derive S256 challenge, store verifier, present verifier on token exchange. The mechanism is stable across every provider that speaks the RFC correctly. A provider that refuses PKCE (or accepts `plain` and does not enforce the binding on the server side) is caught either at boot (when the record is misconfigured) or at operate time (when the token exchange fails); either way the failure is loud, not silent.

alternativesConsidered.name: Accept `plain` when a provider declares only `plain` support
alternativesConsidered.summary: Match the provider's declared method to keep more providers usable.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Trades a documented security property for provider breadth. A provider that only supports `plain` is a provider whose security posture is worse than the blueprint's claimed floor; accepting them silently means the floor is a lie.

alternativesConsidered.name: Make the challenge method a project-config flag
alternativesConsidered.summary: Let the operator declare the method per provider.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Turns a load-bearing security invariant into a config knob the operator can flip without a paper trail. A project-level ADR is the right shape for making the trade explicit.
